sections.title: Name and taxonomic scope
sections.text: Leccinum aurantiacum (Bull.) Gray is a European red-capped scaber stalk or orange oak bolete. A modern revision includes the oak-associated L. quercinum within this name, whereas some older sources applied L. aurantiacum to pale-scabered poplar collections now separated as L. albostipitatum. Thus a host tree or orange cap alone does not settle the name. The European concept should not automatically be applied to similar North American mushrooms.

sections.title: Cap, pores and scabrous stem
sections.text: The cap is typically about 5–15 cm across, initially rounded or strongly convex and later broadly convex to flatter. Its dry, finely felted surface ranges from orange-red and brick red to reddish brown. A key feature is cap skin projecting beyond the tubes as irregular or triangular flaps, often visible even in older specimens. Beneath the cap are tiny pale cream to whitish pores, ageing duller or brownish and sometimes greying after bruising, never true gills. The solid pale stem is long and sturdy, with numerous raised scabers: in the European revised concept these are generally reddish from youth and darken to reddish brown, rather than starting pure white.

sections.title: Cut surface, habitat and lookalikes
sections.text: Fresh flesh is white, then may pass through pinkish or wine-grey to grey-violet or blackish on cutting; the stem base can show a bluish or greenish tone. The changes vary with maturity and time and are not a single instant blue reaction. It forms ectomycorrhiza with broadleaf trees: oak, poplar, birch and beech are documented, so the vernacular 'oak' is not a strict host rule. European L. albostipitatum has initially white stem scabers and is particularly associated with poplar; L. versipelle is another orange-capped relative often linked to birch. Fine distinctions can require specialist microscopy and knowledge of the trees nearby.

sections.title: Food safety and conservation
sections.text: The German Mycological Society lists the oak red-cap under L. quercinum with L. aurantiacum as a synonym, but also identifies raw or insufficiently heated rough-stemmed boletes as a cause of gastrointestinal illness; its general advice is thorough cooking. Individual reactions and identification uncertainty remain possible. A North American toxicology report describes one fatal case to which a Leccinum of the broad aurantiacum complex contributed; it does not prove that a confirmed European L. aurantiacum caused the death. Do not eat an unidentified red-capped Leccinum or rely on this plate for a food decision. The German list marks this taxon as specially protected and Red List category G; check local conservation rules before collecting.

traits: Dry finely felted red-orange to brick-red cap, usually 5–15 cm, with projecting triangular flaps at margin
Underside of tiny pale cream to whitish pores, duller or brown-grey with age; no gills
Long solid pale stem with raised reddish scabers already young, darkening reddish-brown
Cut white flesh gradually pinkish or wine-grey to grey-violet/blackish; occasional blue-green at stem base
Ectomycorrhizal with several broadleaf hosts including oak, poplar, birch and beech
safetyNote: The DGfM lists this European taxon as an edible species under L. quercinum, but rough-stemmed boletes can cause gastrointestinal illness when raw or insufficiently cooked, and individual reactions remain possible. A reported fatality involved an unidentified North American Leccinum in the broad aurantiacum complex, not a proven specimen of this species. Never use a picture for food identification; seek local expert confirmation, cook any approved harvest thoroughly, and seek poison-centre advice if symptoms follow ingestion.
